questions.q: Quantitative data is
questions.why: Quantitative = numbers; qualitative = words and meanings.

questions.q: A sample that represents the population is
questions.why: Representativeness allows generalisation.

questions.q: Positivists prefer
questions.why: Interpretivists prefer qualitative methods.

questions.q: A researcher lets 20 unemployed people talk freely in long, unstructured interviews about their experiences. What is the main strength of this method?
o: High reliability, because it is easy to repeat exactly
High validity, because it gives rich, detailed data in people's own words
The results can easily be generalised to the whole population
The data is quick to turn into statistics
questions.why: Unstructured interviews produce in-depth qualitative data that reflects respondents' real meanings, so validity is high; small samples and lack of standardisation weaken reliability and generalisation.

questions.q: A researcher picks every 10th name from a school register to build a sample. Which sampling method is this?
questions.why: Systematic sampling chooses people at a fixed interval from a sampling frame, such as every 10th name.

long.q: Describe two advantages of using questionnaires in sociological research.
scheme: B1: one advantage, e.g. large samples can be reached quickly and cheaply
B1: developed: so results can be generalised
B1: a second advantage, e.g. standardised questions give reliable, comparable data
B1: developed: easy to analyse statistically

long.q: Read the source. 'A researcher wanted to study the experiences of teenagers who work part-time. She posted a questionnaire on a social media page for students and received 400 replies. 70% of those who replied were girls, and most lived in one city.' (a) Identify two weaknesses of the sample in the source. (b) Suggest one way the researcher could make her sample more representative, and explain why it would help.
scheme: B1: a weakness: a self-selected (volunteer) sample of people who use that social media page, who may not be typical
B1: a second weakness: gender imbalance (70% girls) or most respondents from one city
B1: an improvement, e.g. stratified or quota sampling by gender and region, or random sampling from school registers
B1: explained: the sample then reflects the wider population of teenagers, so findings can be generalised

long.q: What is meant by the term 'triangulation'?
scheme: B1: using more than one research method (or source of data, or researcher) to study the same topic
B1: so that findings can be cross-checked, improving validity and reliability

long.q: Explain why some sociologists prefer to use unstructured interviews.
scheme: B1: flexible: the interviewer can follow up and probe answers
B1: rapport and trust lead to more honest, detailed answers
B1: rich qualitative data with high validity
B1: people describe their views in their own words, which interpretivists value (understanding meanings)
B1: suitable for sensitive topics
B1: can reveal issues the researcher had not thought of in advance

long.q: To what extent is it possible for sociological research to be objective?
scheme: B1: objectivity means research free from the researcher's bias and values
B1: for: positivists argue scientific methods (standardised questionnaires, statistics) reduce the researcher's influence
B1: for: peer review and replication help check for bias
B1: against: the researcher's values affect the choice of topic and the interpretation of results
B1: against: interviewer bias, and people changing their behaviour when observed
B1: against: funding bodies or governments may influence what is researched and published
B1: interpretivists argue complete objectivity is impossible, so researchers should be reflexive and open about their values
B1: a reasoned judgement on the extent

questions.q: Norms are
questions.why: Norms guide everyday behaviour.

questions.q: Primary socialisation mainly takes place in
questions.why: In early childhood, within the family.

questions.q: What are norms?
questions.why: Values are beliefs about what is important.

questions.q: A boy is told 'boys don't cry' and given toy cars, while his sister is given dolls and praised for being gentle. What does this illustrate?
o: Secondary socialisation by the peer group
Gender role socialisation in the family
questions.why: Parents are teaching different expected behaviours to boys and girls during primary socialisation, which is gender role socialisation.

questions.q: A group of young people share their own music, clothes and slang but still accept most of society's main values. This group is best described as…
questions.why: A subculture has some distinctive norms and values within the wider culture; a counter-culture actively rejects mainstream values.

long.q: Describe two ways in which the peer group socialises young people.
scheme: B1: one way, e.g. peer pressure encourages conformity to group norms (dress, music, language)
B1: developed: those who don't conform face informal sanctions such as teasing or exclusion
B1: a second way, e.g. peers act as role models for attitudes and behaviour
B1: developed: this shapes identity, e.g. through youth subcultures

long.q: What is meant by the term 'cultural diversity'?
scheme: B1: the existence of a variety of different cultures or cultural groups within one society
B1: e.g. differences in ethnicity, religion, language and customs in a multicultural society

long.q: Describe two ways in which schools socialise children.
scheme: B1: the hidden curriculum
B1: described: pupils learn punctuality, obedience and respect for authority through school routines
B1: the formal curriculum, or rewards and sanctions
B1: described: e.g. lessons in national history and citizenship pass on shared values; detentions and praise reinforce norms

long.q: Explain how the media can influence gender identity.
scheme: B1: stereotyped representations, e.g. women shown as carers or judged on appearance, men as strong and active
B1: role models: young people copy celebrities and influencers
B1: advertising targets genders separately, e.g. toys and clothes in 'pink' and 'blue' ranges
B1: repeated images make gender norms seem natural and normal
B1: an example or evidence, e.g. beauty ideals on social media linked to body image
B1: recognition of change: more varied representations can challenge stereotypes

long.q: To what extent do young people today have a free choice over their identity?
scheme: B1: identity: a person's sense of who they are and how others see them
B1: choice: postmodernists argue people 'pick and mix' identities through consumption and lifestyle
B1: choice: social media lets young people create and present online identities
B1: choice: hybrid identities among young people from minority ethnic backgrounds
B1: constraint: social class limits what people can afford to buy or do
B1: constraint: gender, ethnicity and age are partly ascribed, and others label us
B1: constraint: socialisation by family and religion shapes values strongly
B1: a reasoned judgement on the extent

questions.q: Social mobility means
questions.why: Upward or downward mobility.

questions.q: A meritocracy is a system where rewards are based on
questions.why: Functionalists claim modern societies are meritocratic.

questions.q: What is social mobility?
o: Movement of people between social classes
Changing jobs at the same level
questions.why: It can be upward or downward, within or between generations.

questions.q: The daughter of a factory worker becomes a doctor. What type of social mobility is this?
questions.why: Her position is compared with her parent's, across generations, and she has moved to a higher-status occupation.

questions.q: Which is an example of relative poverty rather than absolute poverty?
o: A family lacks enough food to stay healthy
A family has no access to clean drinking water
A family cannot afford the school trips and holidays that most families in their society take
questions.why: Relative poverty is judged against the normal living standards of a society; the other options describe a lack of basic needs, which is absolute poverty.

long.q: Explain two ways in which social class can affect a person's life chances.
scheme: B1: one way, e.g. health: working-class people tend to have lower life expectancy
B1: developed: e.g. poorer housing and diet, less access to private healthcare
B1: a second way, e.g. education: middle-class children are more likely to reach university
B1: developed: e.g. cultural capital, paying for tutors, or moving near high-performing schools

long.q: What is meant by the term 'social mobility'?
scheme: B1: movement of individuals or groups up or down the stratification system (e.g. between social classes)
B1: it can be intergenerational (compared with parents) or intragenerational (within a person's own lifetime)

long.q: Describe two features of the caste system.
scheme: B1: a feature, e.g. status is ascribed at birth
B1: described: it cannot be changed by achievement, so it is a closed system with little mobility
B1: a second feature, e.g. endogamy or rules of ritual purity
B1: described: e.g. marriage only within one's caste maintains boundaries; restrictions on contact are justified by religious ideas of purity and pollution

long.q: Explain why poverty may continue across generations.
scheme: B1: a cycle of deprivation: poor diet and housing harm health and education
B1: material deprivation limits educational success, leading to low-paid work
B1: the culture of poverty (Oscar Lewis): fatalistic values passed on through socialisation
B1: structural explanations: lack of jobs, low wages, the poverty trap
B1: lack of cultural and social capital (useful contacts and knowledge)
B1: the 'underclass' view (Murray): welfare dependency passed from parents to children

long.q: To what extent has gender inequality in the workplace been reduced?
scheme: B1: laws on equal pay and against discrimination (e.g. the UK Equal Pay Act 1970)
B1: more women in paid work and higher education
B1: more women in professional and managerial jobs
B1: a continuing gender pay gap
B1: the glass ceiling: few women in the most senior posts
B1: horizontal and vertical segregation: women concentrated in lower-paid sectors such as care and retail
B1: the dual burden and part-time work linked to childcare
B1: a reasoned judgement on the extent

questions.q: A nuclear family consists of
questions.why: The extended family includes wider kin.

questions.q: What is a nuclear family?
o: Two parents and their dependent children
questions.why: The extended family includes other relatives.

questions.q: Which is evidence of family diversity?
o: Growth of single-parent and same-sex families
questions.why: Explain why the change has happened.

questions.q: Two divorced parents remarry and live together with the children from both of their previous marriages. What type of family is this?
questions.why: A reconstituted (blended) family is formed when adults with children from earlier relationships form a new household.

questions.q: Which is a likely reason for the rise in divorce rates in many societies?
o: Women becoming more financially dependent on men
Laws making divorce easier and cheaper to obtain
questions.why: Legal changes have lowered the cost and difficulty of divorce; the other options would make divorce less likely.

long.q: 'The nuclear family is no longer the main family type.' Evaluate this view. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: for: growth of lone-parent families, e.g. through divorce or choice
B1: for: other diverse types, e.g. reconstituted, same-sex, cohabiting, single-person households
B1: for: supported with a theorist or trend, e.g. the Rapoports on family diversity
B1: against: most people still live in a nuclear family at some stage of life
B1: against: e.g. Chester's 'neo-conventional family': the nuclear form has adapted rather than disappeared
B1: a reasoned judgement that follows from the points made

long.q: What is meant by the term 'extended family'?
scheme: B1: a family that includes relatives beyond parents and children, e.g. grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins
B1: living together or nearby with regular contact (vertically or horizontally extended)

long.q: Describe two functions of the family according to functionalists.
scheme: B1: primary socialisation
B1: described: children learn the basic norms and values of society
B1: a second function, e.g. stabilisation of adult personalities (Parsons), reproduction or economic support
B1: described: e.g. the family gives adults emotional security that helps them cope with the stresses of work

long.q: Explain why the average age of first marriage has increased in many societies.
scheme: B1: more people stay in higher education for longer
B1: women's careers and financial independence
B1: cohabitation is widely accepted, so many couples live together first
B1: the cost of weddings and housing
B1: secularisation: less religious pressure to marry young
B1: individualisation: people want to establish themselves and find the 'right' partner first

long.q: To what extent are conjugal roles now equal?
scheme: B1: for: the symmetrical family (Young and Willmott)
B1: for: more women in paid work and men doing more childcare and housework
B1: for: the idea of the 'new man'
B1: against: Oakley found women still did most housework
B1: against: women's dual burden of paid work and domestic work
B1: against: emotion work, or the 'triple shift'
B1: against: men often control major decisions and money (e.g. Pahl)
B1: a reasoned judgement, recognising variation by class, ethnicity and generation

questions.q: The 'hidden curriculum' is
o: the values and attitudes learned informally at school
questions.why: e.g. punctuality, obedience.

questions.q: What is the hidden curriculum?
o: Values and attitudes taught informally through school life
questions.why: For example punctuality and obedience.

questions.q: How might material deprivation affect educational achievement?
o: Lack of resources such as books, space or food can lower attainment
questions.why: Cultural factors and labelling in school also matter.

questions.q: A teacher expects a pupil to do badly, gives them less attention, and the pupil's work gets worse. What concept describes this?
questions.why: The teacher's label shapes how the pupil is treated, and the pupil comes to live up to the prediction.

questions.q: Middle-class parents use their knowledge of how schools work to choose the best school and help with homework. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.why: Cultural capital is the knowledge, attitudes and skills, often passed on by middle-class families, that give children an advantage in education.

long.q: Explain why girls have tended to outperform boys at school in many countries.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. changing employment opportunities and aspirations for women
B1: developed: girls see qualifications as the route to a career (e.g. Sharpe's study of girls' changing priorities)
B1: a second reason, e.g. boys' anti-school or 'laddish' subcultures
B1: developed: being seen to work hard is 'uncool', so boys put in less effort

long.q: What is meant by the term 'cultural capital'?
scheme: B1: the knowledge, attitudes, tastes and skills valued by the education system (Bourdieu)
B1: more often held by middle-class families, giving their children an advantage at school

long.q: Describe two ways in which setting or streaming can affect students.
scheme: B1: labelling: students in lower sets are seen as less able
B1: described: lower teacher expectations can lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy of lower achievement
B1: top sets get more demanding work and are entered for higher-tier exams
B1: described: bottom-set students may form anti-school subcultures, widening the gap (e.g. Lacey, Ball)

long.q: Explain how private education may reproduce social inequality.
scheme: B1: fees mean only wealthier families can afford it
B1: smaller classes and better resources lead to higher results
B1: higher entry rates to elite universities
B1: social networks and contacts that lead to top jobs
B1: cultural capital: confidence, manners and tastes valued by elites
B1: elite self-recruitment: a large share of top judges, politicians and executives attended private schools, so privilege passes between generations

long.q: To what extent does education provide equal opportunities for all?
scheme: B1: for: free, compulsory schooling and exams open to all (a meritocracy)
B1: for: functionalists argue education allocates roles by ability
B1: against: class differences in achievement linked to material deprivation
B1: against: middle-class cultural capital is rewarded
B1: against: gender differences, e.g. in subject choice
B1: against: ethnicity, e.g. labelling or an ethnocentric curriculum
B1: against: parental choice and fee-paying schools favour wealthier families
B1: a reasoned judgement on the extent

questions.q: Deviance is
o: behaviour that goes against social norms
questions.why: Deviance need not be criminal.

questions.q: Formal social control includes
questions.why: Informal control comes from family, peers and community.

questions.q: What is deviance?
o: Behaviour that goes against a society's norms
questions.why: Not all deviance is criminal.

questions.q: What is the dark figure of crime?
o: Crime that is not reported or recorded
questions.why: So official statistics are incomplete.

questions.q: A teenager is called a 'troublemaker' by teachers and police, starts to see himself that way, and commits more crime. Which explanation fits best?
o: Labelling leading to a self-fulfilling prophecy
questions.why: Interactionists argue that a label can change a person's self-image so that they act out the label, increasing deviance.

long.q: Explain why some social groups appear more often in official crime statistics.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. police target certain groups (labelling, stereotyping)
B1: developed with how this raises recorded crime
B1: a second reason, e.g. material deprivation or subcultures
B1: developed with a link to evidence or a theorist

long.q: What is meant by the term 'deviance'?
scheme: B1: behaviour that goes against the norms or expectations of a society or group
B1: it is not always illegal, and what counts as deviant varies over time and between cultures

long.q: Describe two agencies of formal social control.
scheme: B1: the police
B1: described: enforce the law by investigating crime, arresting and cautioning offenders
B1: a second agency, e.g. the courts or prisons
B1: described: e.g. courts decide guilt and pass sentences; prisons punish and try to rehabilitate

long.q: Explain why some crimes are not reported to the police.
scheme: B1: the victim may not know a crime has happened, e.g. fraud or white-collar crime
B1: the crime seems too trivial to report
B1: fear of revenge from the offender
B1: embarrassment or stigma, e.g. sexual offences or domestic violence
B1: distrust of the police, or a belief that nothing will be done
B1: 'victimless' or consensual crimes, e.g. drug use, have no one to report them: all of this creates the 'dark figure' of crime

long.q: To what extent is crime caused by poverty?
scheme: B1: for: Merton's strain theory: blocked opportunities lead some to 'innovate' through crime
B1: for: material deprivation linked to property crime
B1: for: subcultural theory, e.g. Cohen's status frustration among working-class boys
B1: for: Marxists: capitalism creates crime and the law is enforced selectively against the poor
B1: against: white-collar and corporate crime is committed by the wealthy
B1: against: official statistics over-represent the poor because of policing and labelling
B1: against: other factors such as gender, age, peer groups and opportunity
B1: a reasoned judgement on the extent

questions.q: A 'moral panic' is
o: an exaggerated public reaction to a group seen as a threat
questions.why: Cohen's study of Mods and Rockers.

questions.q: What is a moral panic?
o: Exaggerated media reaction to a group seen as a threat
questions.why: Cohen's folk devils.

questions.q: What is agenda-setting by the media?
o: Choosing which issues the public thinks about
questions.why: Gatekeepers decide what is reported.

questions.q: The owners of a newspaper make sure it never criticises their other businesses or their political allies. Which view of the media does this support?
questions.why: Marxists argue that powerful owners control media content to protect their own interests and ideas.

questions.q: Teenagers say they watch a talent show so they can relax and chat about it with friends the next day. Which model of media effects does this support?
questions.why: The uses and gratifications model sees audiences as active, choosing media to meet their own needs such as relaxation and social interaction.

long.q: Describe how the media can create a moral panic.
scheme: B1: exaggerated or sensationalised reporting of a group or event
B1: the group is labelled as 'folk devils', a threat to society's values
B1: public concern grows and moral entrepreneurs demand action, e.g. tougher laws or policing
B1: an example or theorist, e.g. Cohen's study of Mods and Rockers

long.q: What is meant by the term 'gatekeeping'?
scheme: B1: the power of editors, journalists or owners to decide which stories are reported and which are left out
B1: this shapes what audiences know and think about

long.q: Describe two ways in which social media has changed how news is produced.
scheme: B1: citizen journalism: ordinary people film and report events
B1: described: eyewitness accounts can appear before professional journalists arrive
B1: news spreads instantly, and journalists find stories on social media
B1: described: there is pressure to publish quickly, with less checking, so fake news can spread

long.q: Explain how the media may represent women in stereotypical ways.
scheme: B1: a focus on appearance and the sexualisation of women's bodies (e.g. Mulvey's 'male gaze')
B1: domestic and caring roles in advertising
B1: under-representation as experts and in sports coverage
B1: symbolic annihilation (Tuchman): women ignored or trivialised
B1: older women especially under-represented
B1: recognition of change: more strong, varied female characters in recent media

long.q: To what extent do the media have a direct effect on audience behaviour?
scheme: B1: the hypodermic syringe model: media messages are 'injected' into a passive audience
B1: evidence: Bandura's Bobo doll experiment, where children copied violence they had seen
B1: claims of 'copycat' behaviour after violent films or games
B1: against: the two-step flow model (Katz and Lazarsfeld): opinion leaders filter messages
B1: against: uses and gratifications: audiences are active and choose media for their own needs
B1: cultivation theory (Gerbner): effects are long-term and gradual rather than direct
B1: criticism: laboratory experiments like Bandura's are artificial and lack ecological validity
B1: a reasoned judgement on the extent
